nameStory: The white-faced storm-petrel gets its name from the distinctive white facial markings that stand out against its darker plumage, making it look like it's wearing a pale mask. Storm-petrels as a group earned their dramatic name from sailors who noticed these small seabirds seemed to dance across the waves during rough weather, as if they were walking on water during storms.
description: The white-faced storm-petrel is a small seabird about the size of a large swallow that spends most of its life far out at sea. It has distinctive white facial markings that create a masked appearance against its darker body, with long wings adapted for gliding over ocean waves. These petrels are extremely rare visitors to New England waters, with only one recorded observation in the region. They're built for life on the open ocean, with tube-shaped nostrils and specialized glands for processing salt water.

idTips.label: White facial pattern
idTips.description: Bold white markings on the face and forehead create a distinctive masked appearance that stands out even at a distance against the bird's darker cap and back

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a bouncing, erratic pattern close to the water surface, appearing to skip or dance across the waves with shallow wingbeats

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Small and delicate, about swallow-sized with proportionally long, narrow wings that appear almost translucent when backlit by sunlight

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Bright yellowish or orange legs that often dangle below the body during flight, sometimes appearing to touch the water surface

idTips.label: Ocean habitat
idTips.description: Found only over open ocean waters, never near shore or inland, usually far from any visible land

habitat: White-faced storm-petrels are found exclusively over deep ocean waters, far from shore in the open Atlantic. In the extremely rare instances they might be seen in New England waters, it would be during pelagic birding trips many miles offshore. They prefer areas where deep, nutrient-rich waters bring small fish and plankton to the surface.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen, but any sightings would occur during migration periods over deep offshore waters during pelagic birding expeditions.
seasonality.summer: Potential for vagrant individuals during the peak of their activity season, though still extraordinarily rare in New England waters.
seasonality.fall: Slight possibility during post-breeding dispersal when some individuals might wander far from their normal range into North Atlantic waters.
seasonality.winter: Generally absent from New England waters during this season when most individuals are in southern hemisphere breeding areas.

funFact: White-faced storm-petrels can actually "walk" on water by rapidly pattering their feet on the surface while their wings keep them aloft, allowing them to pick up tiny fish and plankton without ever fully landing - it's like they're doing a high-speed tap dance on the ocean!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other storm-petrel species, but the distinctive white facial markings are unique among storm-petrels. Wilson's storm-petrels, more common in New England waters, lack the white face pattern and have different flight behaviors.
contextualKnowledge: The single observation count in New England reflects just how rare this species is in our region - they're primarily birds of the southern oceans around Australia, New Zealand, and South Atlantic islands, making any New England sighting an exceptional vagrant record that would excite birders across the region.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus Pelagodroma, the white-faced storm-petrel is quite distinct from other storm-petrels. Compared to the more familiar Wilson's and Leach's storm-petrels found in New England waters, it has unique white facial markings and different feeding behavior, often appearing to walk on water rather than diving or surface-dipping. Its flight is also more erratic and bouncing compared to the steadier flight patterns of its relatives.
